doc.title: Ray Ricker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 27, 2022

title: Designing the jazz curriculum at Eastman
summary: Ricker, Ray Wright and Bill Dobbins built the jazz major, winning over colleagues; Rowe notes jazz majors fill symphony parts more easily.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: When it came time to construct a four year curriculum for a jazz major, how many people were involved in those decisions about what courses are going to be required? What are things you can choose from? And what was really important? I imagine you were in the middle of that?

Well yeah but that was quite a while ago. Thirty years probably you know. But I know it was figured out with mainly the three of us: Ray Wright, Bill Dobbins, and myself. Now those two guys were full time on the jazz side of things. I was teaching, you know, one- on-one saxophone lessons and clarinet to begin with and teaching ten hours of jazz which was an improvisation course and direct a band, that kind of thing. Probably a couple of courses, improv courses. So Ray and Bill mainly put it together with my input. And then outside of that we brought in people from the wind/brass/percussion department, you know like John Marcellus on trombone and the trumpet people, and the people that would be influenced, would be affected by this. And then we had to find some people who were sympathetic on rhythm section kind of instruments. Not that they would teach it but they just have to say hey that’s okay and it’s a thing to do and yes, it’s fine. So we got friends and we talked to them and when it came time for, well I said the first time we had that undergrad thing not everybody voted for it. It wasn’t unanimous but it got started. So the main thing is we started with a small group, expanded it out, made friends, and told them what we were doing. And by then the quality was really, really high. And you can’t argue with that you know. If the example is extremely high and these guys were doing things — I mean the theory people would say man we love these jazz guys when they come in to the theory, you know they do so well. You know they were really supportive. You

know and then there was a couple of, at least one, musicologist — he was theory. But he was a pianist, an old jazz piano player that had done it. So he was really on top of it. He ended up teaching a course on Bill Evans that was very popular and really, really good. You know.

I wish I could remember who said this to me but they pointed out that today’s jazz major, instrumentalist, is much more likely to be able to step into a symphony gig and fill a part, rather than the other way around. That an orchestral musician would have much more trouble going playing Thad Jones/Mel Lewis charts.
Yeah I think that’s true, yeah, really. Definitely.
